summary:
The U.S. data center policy landscape remains in a period of rapid local escalation layered over consequential state-level pauses. Twenty-two states now carry active restrictions of some form, and the last week of October 2026 reinforced the pattern: major cities are no longer outliers. San Diego became the largest city yet to pause data center development — Mayor Todd Gloria signed an executive order on October 22 and the City Council unanimously ratified a 45-day moratorium on October 27, prompted by a reported 400 MW proposal at the Navy's NAVWAR site — while Charlotte, whose 150-day moratorium was set to expire November 5, voted unanimously on October 26 to extend it through October 18, 2027. New county-level pauses were enacted in Tazewell County, Illinois (nine months, through July 2027) and Ascension Parish, Louisiana (90 days), and Pittsburg, California adopted a 45-day pause aimed at the next phases of the AVAIO campus.

The statewide pictures in New York and Texas — the two most significant state-level interventions — held steady but showed new texture. New York's Executive Order 62 moratorium on 50 MW+ facilities remains in force, while the broader Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) still has not been delivered to Governor Hochul, who must act by December 31 once it is; the bill's fate is becoming a notable political question heading into year-end. In Texas, Governor Abbott's September directive halting TCEQ permits for data center projects showed enforcement gaps: the agency issued an air permit to Sitespan LLC on October 13 despite the pause, then suspended it under public scrutiny and announced it is shutting down automatic permit filing to review data center applications manually. ERCOT's grid audit, the trigger for lifting the Texas freeze, is still expected around mid-December.

Courts and ballot boxes are emerging as the next battlegrounds. Frederick County, Maryland's moratorium survived its first legal test in late October when a judge denied Quantum Maryland's request for a temporary restraining order — Quantum claims at least $500 million in lost real estate value — with a preliminary injunction hearing set for November 10. In Ohio, 18 communities have data center measures on the November 3 ballot, including an outright ban in Hubbard and a referendum in Ashville on repealing exemptions from the village moratorium, making this the first election cycle in which data center policy is being decided directly by voters at scale. Data center siting has also become a visible issue in the 2026 midterm and gubernatorial races.

Trends to watch: first, the moratorium-to-ordinance pipeline is maturing — Kirksville, Fayetteville, Davidson County and Jefferson County all converted pauses or debates into permanent zoning standards this week, typically industrial-district confinement, large residential setbacks, noise caps and cooling-water limits, and Arlington, Texas and Hutchinson, Kansas have similar rules in the pipeline. Second, bans on water-intensive cooling are spreading as a standard tool (Gilbert, Arizona's proposed ban on open-loop evaporative cooling and potable cooling water echoes conditions Oklahoma City attached to its first approved mega-campus). Third, watch the November votes queued up in Aurora, Colorado (indefinite moratorium), Springfield, Missouri (extension to February), Harmony, Minnesota, and Ellington, Connecticut, along with South Carolina's drafting of a closed-loop-cooling and siting bill for the 2027 session — signs that the next legislative wave is already forming.
